claims.text: Metadynamics-driven phase-transition sampling with suitable collective variables can accurately estimate melting properties of high-melting refractory materials.
The method can estimate melting temperature, entropy of fusion, enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at melting.
Metadynamics will significantly reduce computational cost relative to full ab initio free-energy methods.
The initial simulated state contains coexisting solid and liquid regions near the melting conditions.
Collective variables such as local structural order parameters or coordination numbers can distinguish the solid phase from the liquid phase.
Depositing metadynamics bias every 500–1000 fs accelerates solid–liquid phase transitions.
Periodic deposition of biasing Gaussians promotes transitions between solid and liquid states.
Sampling bias-driven transitions enables reconstruction of the free-energy surface.
Energy discontinuities across the phase transition can be used to extract the enthalpy of fusion.
Free-energy differences can be used to derive the entropy change on fusion.
Volume discontinuities across the phase transition can be used to extract the volume change at melting.
Energy and volume discontinuities across the transition can be used to determine the melting temperature.
Metadynamics-derived melting properties will be comparable in accuracy to results from full ab initio free-energy integration.
The reduced computational cost will make the method suitable for high-throughput studies.
Full ab initio molecular dynamics with thermodynamic integration is accurate but computationally prohibitive for high-throughput applications.
Metadynamics accuracy may be limited when the collective variables do not capture the distinct solid and liquid atomic arrangements.
Poorly tuned bias-deposition parameters may limit the method's accuracy.
Extreme temperatures or highly disordered systems may reduce the reliability of the method.
